name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Oklahoma CareerTech board to vote on request for funding increase
description: OKLAHOMA CITY — A state board governing vocational learning centers could ask for a $67.87 million budget increase next year with the goal of expanding workforce training. The Oklahoma Department of Career and Technology Education on Thursday presented a $249.56 million budget request for the 2028 fiscal year. The agency’s board is expected to vote […]
text:
An entrance to an Oklahoma CareerTech office in Stillwater is pictured on Dec. 6, 2024. (Photo by Emma Murphy/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY — A state board governing vocational learning centers could ask for a $67.87 million budget increase next year with the goal of expanding workforce training.
The Oklahoma Department of Career and Technology Education on Thursday presented a $249.56 million budget request for the 2028 fiscal year. The agency’s board is expected to vote next month on whether to send the proposal to the state Legislature for consideration.
“What we need is everybody to understand the confidence that we have in our system and the state should have in our system,” state CareerTech director Brent Haken said while presenting the budget proposal. “There is nobody still, even though we’ve got a lot of work to do, that shows the return on investment that we do when we get students into the program.”
Brent Haken, state director of Oklahoma CareerTech, speaks to attendees of an open house at the Metro Tech Aviation Campus on June 21, 2024. (Photo by Emma Murphy/Oklahoma Voice)
Oklahoma’s 29 CareerTech centers count more than 500,000 enrollments across the state in job skill programs, adult education and K-12 courses. The state agency has asked for significant funding increases in recent years to reduce waitlists, which in 2024 counted 7,500 students.
State lawmakers appropriated more than $185 million to the CareerTech system for the current fiscal year, tens of millions of dollars less than the agency had requested.
With his latest budget ask, Haken suggested Oklahoma needs to invest far more than its current CareerTech funding levels to keep pace with other states.
“We are seeing other states make significant advancements in (CareerTech education) above what Oklahoma is doing,” he said during the meeting. “So we’re going to have to figure out how we want to play ball in that arena if we want to continue to have the system that we do.”
His proposal includes a $27.65 million increase to postsecondary workforce training, including $18.65 million in recurring funding to remove waitlists.
An additional $20 million would help “build a statewide approach” to giving more students in grades 5-12 career exposure at vocational technology centers, according to the agency’s proposal.
The agency reported 35% of all Oklahoma students in fifth through 12th grade had enrolled in a CareerTech class. Among high school juniors, that number recently surpassed 50%, Haken said.
His budget request would seek a one-time appropriation of $10 million to add more CareerTech centers in areas that don’t yet have one. 
Haken said the state took a similar approach when it expanded into Beaver County. It offered funds to start programs and support the new center for its first year so “they didn’t have to wait on tax money to come in,” he said
CareerTech centers rely on local tax revenue, state appropriations and federal funds.
“We still have significant white space across the state where we could use those dollars to bring people into the system,” Haken said. “If they do decide to come into the system, then we have a tax base that sustains it, but this would be a one-time request.”
An added $6.7 million would support curriculum costs, new programs and CareerTech student organizations, according to the proposal.
The cost of employees’ insurance benefits is expected to rise by $3.72 million, which the state is obligated to pay, Haken said.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Minneapolis looks to close as many as 16 schools amid declining enrollment
description: Minneapolis Public Schools is taking the first steps toward closing as many as 16 schools after years of declining enrollment has left it with an expansive real estate portfolio that includes more than 12,000 empty desks. District leaders unveiled on Tuesday three options for school closures, which they say will allow them to provide more […]
text:
(Photo by Will Jacott/Minnesota Reformer)Minneapolis Public Schools is taking the first steps toward closing as many as 16 schools after years of declining enrollment has left it with an expansive real estate portfolio that includes more than 12,000 empty desks.
District leaders unveiled on Tuesday three options for school closures, which they say will allow them to provide more consistent educational offerings, like art and music. School leaders didn’t mention the budget concerns looming over the district — a $39.7 million deficit this year — or even how much the proposals might save.
“We’ve been talking for a long time about the challenges facing our district,” Superintendent Lisa Sayles-Adams told the board Tuesday. “Tonight, after years of analysis, listening and planning, we will be looking at what we might actually do about it.”
At the earliest, the board will vote to select a plan in November, after school board elections, but before families begin the enrollment process for next school year. The board could also choose to make no changes. The district has been discussing the potential for school closures, calling the process “transformation,” since 2023.
School closures face fierce opposition from many parents, who don’t want to see their neighborhood school shutter, as well as the powerful teachers’ union, which fears consolidation will lead to further enrollment declines.
In a press release, the Minneapolis Federation of Educators called the proposals “three different worst-case scenarios for the future of MPS.” The district did not include any information on which jobs, if any, would be eliminated as part of their proposals.
Across all three options presented Tuesday, the district proposes closing seven elementary schools — Bethune, Pratt, Lake Harriet Lower Campus, Lake Nokomis Wenonah, Loring, Kenny and Hmong International Academy — and a single middle school, Anwatin. Five additional elementary schools would be closed in one or two of the options presented — Field, Hiawatha, Howe, Webster and Cityview.
None of the proposals include closing any of the district’s seven community high schools. But under all options, the district would relocate four of its specialized high school programs, currently located in their own separate buildings, within existing community high schools.
Heritage High School, which focuses on Somali language and culture, would relocate to Edison High School. Longfellow High School, which serves pregnant and parenting students, would relocate to North High School, which also serves these students. FAIR, an arts magnet high school, would relocate to North. Wellstone, which provides legally mandated services for immigrant students ages 18-22, would relocate from leased space at Minneapolis College into South High School.
Minneapolis Public Schools assessed $5.3 million in tax penalties in past four years

The district’s estimates 12-14% of students would be impacted by the proposals.
The proposed closures would happen across the city, but be particularly pronounced in the north and southwest parts of the city. Both areas would lose two elementary schools under all three options. Schools that feed students to Washburn High School would be the least impacted under the three options, while also retaining the highest enrollment compared to any other area of the city.
The plan expands the Montessori program at Seward from K-6 to K-8. In two scenarios, Kenwood Elementary School would be moved back to the Southwest High School from North, reversing an unpopular attempt five years ago to integrate what was a predominantly white elementary school into a predominantly Black high school.
Principals at the schools proposed for closure were notified shortly before the board meeting Tuesday night.
In January, the district laid out what it considers the minimum level of enrollment necessary to support the minimum level of services schools should provide. For elementary schools, the minimum size ranges from 360 to 477, depending on the number of low-income students enrolled at the school. At the middle school level, the range is 594 to 756, and at the high school level the range is 888 to 1064.
Community engagement sessions are scheduled in September and October across the district, and there is also an online survey. The board will hear a summary of feedback on Oct. 20.
The district promised Tuesday that if one of the three options were enacted, it would be able to guarantee sufficient funding going forward to provide a consistent set of services across all schools. The only specific staffing the district promised, however, was at least two academic intervention teachers per building, and full-time art, music and gym teachers at all elementary schools.
The district has struggled for many years to provide some basic services, like elementary art, music and gym, at its lowest-enrolled schools.
The district presented only limited information on the financial impact of closing schools. Deputy Superintendent Ty Thompson said that addressing the district’s long-term financial challenges was not part of the board’s directive on “transformation” to the superintendent.
The district’s finances have been deteriorating since 2018, according to its annual financial projections. The district was able to delay budget cuts when it received over $264 million in federal pandemic aid. It used much of the money to prop up its sprawling portfolio of schools which have capacity for around 42,000 students, while the district’s enrollment is below 30,000.
A combination of reasons have left the district in an ongoing cycle of cuts in recent years. Some factors outside the district’s control include education funding that hasn’t kept up with inflation,  state funding that doesn’t cover the full cost of mandated English learner and special education services, and new unfunded state mandates like paid medical and family leave and summer unemployment benefits for some school workers.
But the district has also failed to manage many of the financial levers within its control. It made a series of blunders that led to steep enrollment losses and the associated funding, including keeping schools closed during the pandemic longer than any other in the state.
The district also implemented an unpopular plan that redrew boundaries to reduce segregation while closing popular magnet schools in the district’s wealthy Southwest corner.

The district has failed to control its labor costs, agreeing to significant pay raises and mandated staffing levels that have raised its costs faster than its funding has increased.
And, the district has made several multi-million dollar financial errors which the Reformer has uncovered this year.
Minneapolis is not the only district closing schools in the state. St. Paul Public Schools voted to close six public schools in 2021, and Robbinsdale Public Schools started this school year with three fewer school buildings.
The same factors at play in Minnesota are also impacting districts across the country. In recent years, Oakland, San Francisco, Los Angeles, Seattle, Portland, Denver, Chicago, Houston, San Antonio, Memphis, Miami, and thousands of other districts have faced enrollment decreases and cost increases that have led to discussion of school closures, and in some cases action to close schools.

title: Missouri education board declines to seek $300 million increase in school aid
description: The Missouri State Board of Education declined Tuesday to seek the roughly $300 million increase needed to fully fund the state’s public school funding formula next year, opting instead to request lawmakers allocate the same amount schools are receiving this year. The decision came after board members deadlocked over the Department of Elementary and Secondar[...]
text:
The Department of Elementary and Secondary Education's deputy commissioner of financial and administrative services Kyle Kruse, pictured presenting budget recommendations in September of 2025, brought the latest budget request to the State Board of Education for approval Tuesday (Annelise Hanshaw/Missouri Independent).The Missouri State Board of Education declined Tuesday to seek the roughly $300 million increase needed to fully fund the state’s public school funding formula next year, opting instead to request lawmakers allocate the same amount schools are receiving this year.
The decision came after board members deadlocked over the Department of Elementary and Secondary Education’s proposed budget and whether the state should request money officials acknowledge lawmakers are unlikely to provide. 
After the board discussed budget cuts last month, the department’s finance staff brought a “significantly reduced list of requests,” said Kyle Kruse, deputy commissioner of financial services for the education department.
“Last month I mentioned there being a narrow gate through which our requests need to pass in order to make the final budget,” he said. “So we have decided which requests don’t really get through the gate.”
The department cut the amount of general revenue requested in its supplemental budget by more than half, from $159 million to $73 million. Its list of increases and new funding obligations for next fiscal year also fell by nearly $75 million.
Among the items cut were $3 million for maintenance of the department’s data reporting system and $4 million to continue Dolly Parton’s Imagination Library, which provides free books to young children.
For four of the board’s eight voting members, the reductions were not enough.
“I don’t think this is a serious budget,” said Mike Matousek, a board member from Kansas City. “I think we are asking for money that doesn’t exist.”
The state is bracing for budget reductions across departments in years ahead as revenue growth slows and reserve funds are expected to decline. At the same time, the amount required to fully fund Missouri’s public schools is rising.
The amount of money schools receive from the state is determined by a formula set in state law. Changes lawmakers approved in 2024 are being phased in over several years, increasing the formula’s cost.
For the current fiscal year, lawmakers provided about $190 million less than what the formula called for. Another roughly $110 million increase is expected for fiscal 2028, bringing the gap between current funding and the formula’s calculation to about $300 million.
“The question gets down to: Do we ask for money that we know we’re not going to get?” Kerry Casey, a board member from Chesterfield, said. “I think we have an obligation to inform the legislature as to what the full funding would look like.”
Underfunding the formula is a decision for lawmakers to make, Casey said. The board’s duty is to advocate for schools, she said, saying it was unprecedented for the state board to not recommend full funding of the formula.
“I don’t know that the statute implies that the board’s budget request has to mirror the (formula’s) number,” Matousek said. “If this is all predetermined, then what are we even doing here? Why are we even talking about the budget?”
The board ultimately sided with Matousek, directing the department to keep its foundation formula request flat.
Casey requested the education department include a letter with its budget request explaining its “commitment to education” alongside “our respect… for the state of the general revenue.”
“None of this is trying to take away from districts or kids. That’s still our priority,” said board member Vince Schoemehl, of St. Louis. “This is recognizing (financial) realities.”
